title: Who’s Ger Ger? Who’s dear Gerald
html_source: Should read, “Who’s moth moth? Who’s dear Gerald? Dear Ger, that you? O dear, he is Gerald.” This points to the Italian philosopher Giordano Bruno who had an impact on Joyce. Bruno wrote extensively on the art of memory, a loosely organized group of mnemonic techniques and principles, and we see them mentioned in Virag Lipoti’s “testimony” at Bloom’s “trial” three times. But, much more importantly, are the hidden references to Bruno’s doctrine of the coincidence of contraries, by which he means: “Every power in nature or in spirit must evolve an opposite as the sole condition and means of its manifestation; and every opposite is, therefore, a tendency to reunion.” Joyce mentions this in an examination essay he took in Padua in which he adds that Bruno taught that these “contraries” create a power “without which man cannot fulfill himself.” So we see these opposites appearing in minor things such as the inverting of Virag’s name. Giordano Bruno was burned to death for his “heretical” views on February 17, 1600
